title: Ang 575–577: the Ghorian
tomorrow: why would a song for the dead open with the word 'blessed'?

cards: The dhol is already going in the driveway. A cousin is pinning a gold-fringed cloth over a white horse that keeps eating a carrot like none of this concerns him.

The groom climbs up, wobbles, and a wall of phones goes up at once. This is the baraat, the groom's procession, and Punjabi families have old songs for this moment: ghorian, horse songs, sung as he mounts.
On ang 575, Guru Ram Das takes those very songs and quietly asks who is really riding.

teach.b: These hymns sit in raga Vadhans, and the Granth heads them with the folk title: Ghorian.

teach.h: THE BODY IS THE HORSE THE LORD MADE.
teach.b: In paraphrase, Guru Ram Das sings: this body is the horse, and the Lord himself made it. Blessed is the human birth; it comes by great good fortune.
The Guru's word steers it, and on it the rider crosses the hard road to the Beloved's door. Notice what he keeps. The procession stays.

teach.h: THE PROCESSION STAYS; THE MEANING MOVES.
teach.b: The fine horse stays, the decoration stays, the joy stays. What moves is the meaning. The horse is your own body, and the wedding at the end of the road is the soul meeting God.
So in these songs the body isn't a cage to escape.
It's a gift, made with care, the thing you ride home on.
One detail worth passing on: the Granth names these hymns with the same word families use for the songs sung as the groom mounts, and in the Guru's version the rider is every soul, groom or not.
The road the Ghorian sing about is long. Nobody is asked to walk it. You're handed a horse, and told it was made for you on purpose.

how: Sikhs read the Ghorian in the Guru Granth Sahib, in raga Vadhans; some families also sing folk ghorian at home as the groom gets ready to ride in the baraat.

games.why: Guru Ram Das calls the body a horse the Lord made, and the human birth blessed. it isn't the enemy; it's the ride.

practice: Sit tall, the way a rider sits: feet grounded, spine long, hands resting lightly on your thighs as if they held the reins. Stay in that seat for the sit and let the breath move on its own.
Each time your mind runs ahead, come back to the body under you, the horse you were given.
